chain.g: hair, fiber; hair of a tail

ety.text: From Middle English tail, taile, taille, tayil, tayl, tayle, tayll, teil, tæȝel, from Old English tæġel, tæġl (“tail”), from Proto-West Germanic *tagl, from Proto-Germanic *taglą (“hair, fiber; hair of a tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ- (“hair of the tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to tear, fray, shred”).
From Anglo-Norman, probably from a shortened form of entail.

senses.d: The caudal appendage of an animal that is attached to their posterior and near the anus or cloaca.
ex: Most primates have a tail and fangs.

senses.d: An object or part of an object resembling a tail in shape, such as the thongs on a cat-o'-nine-tails; a strand of material hanging from something.
ex: Duretus writes a great praise of the Distill'd waters of those tails that hang on Willow Trees.
Using a thin tapestry needle, weave the warp tails back into the fabric in a warpwise direction and trim off the excess.

senses.d: The back, last, lower, or inferior part of anything.

senses.d: The rear structure of an aircraft, the empennage.

senses.d: One who surreptitiously follows another.

senses.d: To follow or hang to, like a tail; to be attached closely to, as that which can not be evaded.
ex: Nevertheless his bond of two thousand pounds, wherewith he was tailed, continued uncancelled.

senses.d: To follow and observe surreptitiously.
ex: Tail that car!

senses.d: To pull or draw by the tail.
